title: Trump’s Army secretary hunt takes shape as insiders float potential picks
summary: Sean Parnell and Brian Mast are among names floated to replace Dan Driscoll as secretary of the Army after his reported clashes with Pete Hegseth.
story: Ret. Lt. Gen. Keith Kellogg discusses Army Secretary Dan Driscoll submitting his resignation to President Donald Trump, what the leadership shake-up could mean for the U.S. military, and the next phase of the escalating conflict with Iran on 'America Reports.'
The hunt is on for the next secretary of the Army after Dan Driscoll submitted his resignation to the White House, opening a key leadership vacancy atop the nation’s largest military branch.

Driscoll said Wednesday will be his "last full day" serving as Army secretary, adding that serving in the role under President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has been "the honor of a lifetime."
The next Army secretary will inherit a service undergoing a major transformation, with questions over readiness and the Army’s role as the conflict with Iran continues.
ARMY CUTS HELICOPTERS, PUSHES ‘AMAZON FOR WAR’ AS DRONE COMBAT RESHAPES MILITARY

Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll and Sergeant Major of the Army Michael R. Weimer honored Old Dominion University Army ROTC cadets with eight Meritorious Service Medals and two Purple Hearts during a private ceremony on March 22, 2026, recognizing their courage in the March 12 classroom shooting. (Ian Ives/U.S. Army)

Army Undersecretary Mike Obadal could serve as acting secretary once Driscoll’s departure is finalized. A former special operations officer and defense industry executive, Obadal has also taken on a more public-facing role, including speaking at conferences.

In the Trump administration, deputy officials have repeatedly stepped into top leadership roles after resignations or firings— including then-Navy Under Secretary Hung Cao becoming acting Navy secretary after John Phelan’s departure this year.
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman and a senior adviser to Hegseth, has emerged as one potential candidate, according to sources.
PENTAGON FIRES BACK AFTER MARK KELLY ACCUSES PETE HEGSETH OF TARGETING WOMEN AND BLACK MILITARY OFFICERS
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell speaks during a press conference at the Pentagon on Mar. 17, 2025 in Arlington, Virginia. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"A lot of people inside [Office of the Secretary of War] want to see Sean Parnell become the next Secretary of the Army because they’ve worked alongside him and know what he brings to the table," a senior administration official told Fox News Digital.
Parnell, who serves as assistant to the secretary of War for Public Affairs, is a former United States Army captain whose platoon killed over 350 enemy fighters at the height of the Afghan War.

He unsuccessfully ran for the House in 2020 before launching a 2021 campaign for Pennsylvania’s open Senate seat, earning Trump’s endorsement. He later suspended his campaign amid domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife, Laurie Snell, which he denied.
HEGSETH TURNS TABLES ON DEMS AS SPARKS FLY DURING HEARING CLASH: 'I PUT THIS ON YOU'

U.S. President Donald Trump and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth listen to questions from the press during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on July 31, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images)
The senior administration official said Parnell understands the Pentagon and the problems inside from military experience paired with his work at the highest levels of the institution.

"He also understands the importance of working alongside General LeNeve, who has been carrying an enormous load to keep the Army moving, and giving the Army Staff the leadership and support they need to get it back on track," the official said, referring to the acting Army chief of staff.

A senior Pentagon official told Fox News Digital Parnell has "proven time and time again" that he is loyal to the president, citing that Parnell was present at his rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, where Trump was shot.

After the president was removed from the rally, Parnell stayed behind to help others get out, the senior Pentagon official said. Parnell returned with Trump to Butler three months after the assassination attempt.

"Their relationship goes back many, many, years at this point, and it's not just with the president. It's also very senior members of the White House that are with the President every single day," said the senior Pentagon official.
REPUBLICANS DEFY JOHNSON TO ADVANCE DEMOCRAT-BACKED UKRAINE AID

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks Wednesday during a valor upgrade ceremony at the Pentagon's Hall of Heroes in Arlington, Va., for U.S. Marines who served at Abbey Gate in Kabul, Afghanistan, in 2021. (Pool / Fox News)
A third senior administration official told Fox News Digital that "Sean Parnell is 100% focused on the job he was appointed to by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth."

Florida Rep. Brian Mast may also be under consideration, a source with knowledge told Fox News Digital. The Trump-endorsed candidate serves as chairman of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs and previously served in the Army for 12 years.

Driscoll's exit comes after reportedly butting heads with Hegseth over concerns with the administration about the Army’s transformation and readiness, including his belief that Hegseth had hindered those efforts, Fox News Digital previously reported.
Parnell defended Hegseth’s leadership and said the department remains united behind his vision.

"Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength. Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all-time highs," Parnell told Fox News Digital. "Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way."
"The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first," he added.
Democrats and some Republican lawmakers unloaded on Trump and Hegseth over the changes in the Department of War.

North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said Hegseth is "creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks" while ranking Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee Jack Reed of Rhode Island said, "Hegseth is cultivating a culture where dissent is punished and competence is secondary to personal allegiance."
Navy Secretary John Phelan was ousted in April after reportedly clashing with Hegseth over shipbuilding and management.
FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP TO OPEN DIRECT LINE WITH MILITARY FAMILIES IN GROUND-UP READINESS PUSH
Department of War Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a press briefing at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., on March 31, 2026. (Oliver Contreras / AFP via Getty Images)

The White House directed Fox News Digital to DOW when asked for comment.
Fox News Digital reached out to Parnell, Mast, the Army and DOW for comment.

title: Gloria Steinem, feminist writer and activist, dead at 92
summary: Feminist writer and activist Gloria Steinem has died at the age of 92, according to a statement posted on her Instagram page Thursday.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
Feminist writer and activist Gloria Steinem has died at the age of 92, according to a statement posted on her Instagram page Thursday.

"Yesterday, Gloria Steinem passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her," the message read. "Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end."

"Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves. Gloria lived true to her independent spirit, always with curiosity and a great sense of humor," the statement continued.
The statement said Steinem "spent her recent years doing the two things she loved most: being in community with others and writing."
FLASHBACK: GLORIA STEINEM, NOBEL LAUREATES ARRIVE IN NORTH KOREA FOR PEACE MARCH ACROSS DEMILITARIZED ZONE
Gloria Steinem speaks at a women's march in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 21, 2017.  (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

"Gloria loved the tradition of lighting signal fires on hills to light the way to the other side of the mountain. Lighting your own candle for Gloria makes you part of this global and celestial community circle," it added.

Born in Toledo, Ohio, in 1934, Steinem was a "founder of New York and Ms. magazines, and is the author of An Unexpected Life, The Truth Will Set You Free, But First It Will Piss You Off, My Life on the Road, Moving Beyond Words, Revolution from Within, and Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, in addition to many collections and essays," a biography on her website said.

"She co-founded the National Women’s Political Caucus, the Ms. Foundation for Women, the Free to Be Foundation, and the Women’s Media Center in the United States. As links to other countries, she helped found Equality Now, Donor Direct Action, and Direct Impact Africa," it added.

"Among many tributes and honors for her activism, in 2013 she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Barack Obama and in 2019, she received the Freedom Award from the National Civil Rights Museum," the biography continued, noting that "Gloria’s home is the heart of Gloria’s Foundation and has become renowned as a magnetic and life-changing center for feminist and activist thinkers from around the world."

Steinem "helped to found the Women's Action Alliance, a pioneering national information center that specialized in nonsexist, multiracial children's education, and the National Women's Political Caucus, a group that continues to work to advance the numbers of pro-equality women in elected and appointed office at a national and state level."
CELEBRITY ACTIVISTS WHO HAVE MADE A GLOBAL IMPACT
Gloria Steinem attends the WMC 2025 Women's Media Awards at JW Marriott Essex House Hotel on June 5, 2025 in New York City.  (Astrid Stawiarz/Getty Images for The Women's Media Center)

"She also co-founded the Women's Media Center in 2004. She was president and co-founder of Voters for Choice, a pro-choice political action committee for twenty-five years, then with the Planned Parenthood Action Fund when it merged with VFC for the 2004 elections," her website said.
Steinem married businessman and animal rights activist David Bale in September 2000.
Bale, the father of actor Christian Bale, died three years later from primary brain lymphoma.

Steinem began her career as a journalist, notably one who reported, in 1963, on degrading conditions in Hugh Hefner’s Playboy empire, an undercover assignment she came to later regret, according to The Associated Press. She credited a meeting six years later, where women spoke out boldly in favor of abortion rights, with changing her career path.

"That speak-out was the beginning of activism for me," Steinem, who had undergone a secret illegal abortion herself at age 22, told the AP in an email in 2022, reflecting on the reversal of Roe v Wade. "Either our control over our own bodies is equal, regardless of sex or race, or we’re not living in a democracy."

Well into her 80s, Steinem was traveling the globe and speaking out on issues of importance to her. These included everything from genital mutilation to Korean reconciliation, but it was equality for women that took precedence.
"Being a feminist means that you see the world as whole instead of half," she once said. "It shouldn’t need a name, and one day it won’t."
In 2020, her life was the subject of a feature film, "The Glorias, A Life on The Road," based on her 2015 memoir and starring Julianne Moore.
American feminist and activist Gloria Steinem speaks at a rally outside the United Nations in New York City in 1978.  (Bettye Lane/Photo Researchers History/Getty Images)

title: Convicted predators face lifetime barrier under GOP lawmaker’s sweeping victim protection bill
summary: Rep. Abe Hamadeh's, R-Ariz., Kayleigh's Law passed the House unanimously, requiring lifetime no-contact orders for convicted sex crime and violent felony offenders.
story: Rep. Abe Hamadeh, R-Ariz., explains why Kayleigh's Law is personal to him, reflects on the emotional House vote, and details how the bill would protect survivors from repeatedly facing their convicted abusers as it heads to the Senate.

An Arizona congressman is putting convicted predators on notice after the House unanimously backed a bill designed to prevent abusers from dragging their victims back into court years after their crimes.
"Protect the victim. Stop the predator. End the revolving door," Rep. Abe Hamadeh, R-Ariz., wrote on X after the House passed Kayleigh’s Law.
"When a predator is convicted, the court issues a lifetime no-contact order," he added. "Not until probation ends. Not until some judge decides he’s ‘moved on.’ For life."

Hamadeh told Fox News Digital that the legislation would deliver permanent protection to survivors of federal sex crimes and violent felonies by requiring courts to issue lifetime no-contact injunctions against convicted offenders.
TRUMP SIGNS HAWLEY MEASURE ADDING 200 CHILD EXPLOITATION INVESTIGATORS IN LARGEST CRACKDOWN EFFORT YET
"This is a common-sense type of bill where we’re supporting victims, and we’re prioritizing victims over criminals," Hamadeh said.
The Kayleigh’s Law Act of 2026, introduced by Hamadeh as H.R. 8481, passed the House with unanimous support Monday and now heads to the Senate.

The legislation is named after Kayleigh Kozak, an Arizona mother of five who was sexually abused as a child and later forced to return to court when her abuser sought to have a no-contact protection lifted.
Hamadeh said Kozak was hauled back into court 13 years after the abuse, and then had to return again when the man made another attempt the following year.
CALIFORNIA DEMS TRIGGER OUTRAGE AFTER SIDING WITH CONVICTED CHILD SEX OFFENDERS IN SHOCKING VOTE
Rep. Abe Hamadeh, R-Ariz., promised Kayleigh Kozak he would champion her victim-protection measure if elected to Congress. (X/@RepAbeHamadeh)
"Can you imagine that you have to sit across the room from this man?" Hamadeh said. "That’s something a victim should never have to do."
The federal bill would prohibit an offender from contacting the victim directly or indirectly for the rest of the offender’s life, even after prison, probation or supervised release ends.
"When you abuse a child, or you sexually abuse a child, or if you commit a violent offense against them, you should never have to interact with that person ever in their lives," Hamadeh said.

Kozak’s fight for permanent protections grew out of her own experience with Joshua Jacobsen, a former teacher and soccer coach who pleaded guilty to sexual abuse and luring a minor for sexual exploitation. Kozak was 12 years old and one of his students when the abuse occurred, according to FOX 10 Phoenix.
NEWSOM-BACKED LAW LETS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHILD RAPIST SEEK EARLY RELEASE AGAIN AS DA URGES 'STOP THE MADNESS'

Jacobsen was sentenced to six months in jail and lifetime probation. Nearly two decades later, he asked a Maricopa County judge to end that probation, arguing that his conduct over the previous 18 years showed he had reformed and was ready to "move on," the outlet reported.
Kozak returned to court to oppose his request.

"I am living proof that he is capable of sexually harming children," Kozak told the court. "He consciously chose to violate me, and he was convicted of committing a dangerous crime against a child while he was in a position of power."

Jacobsen’s effort ultimately failed. A Maricopa County judge denied his request in June, citing probation violations that included unauthorized contact with children and breaches of chaperone restrictions, according to Arizona’s Family.
Jacobsen remains on lifetime probation under the supervision of Maricopa County Adult Probation.
Kozak celebrated the House vote on X, saying the country was "one step closer" to giving victims of heinous crimes the permanent protection they deserve.
PREP SCHOOL TEACHER FILMED SEX WITH STUDENT SHE WAS TUTORING: ‘NOT MY BEST THINKING’
Joshua Jacobsen remains on lifetime probation after a judge denied his request to end the court supervision in June 2026. (Phoenix Police Department)
"No victim should ever have to endure the hell I had to walk through," she wrote. "When I discovered protection wasn’t permanent, I knew it had to change."
Versions of Kayleigh’s Law have passed in Arizona and Wisconsin. Hamadeh said more than 1,000 Arizona survivors secured lifetime protection during the state law’s first year.

In a statement announcing the House vote, Hamadeh’s office said the legislation aims to end the "legal tug-of-war" that forces survivors to repeatedly face their attackers in court to maintain basic protections.

"Victims should never again have to fill out another form, sit across from their abuser, or look over their shoulder because the sentence ran out, and the system shrugged," Hamadeh said in a statement following the vote.
The issue became personal for Hamadeh long before he entered Congress.
SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS
Hamadeh urged the Senate to approve Kayleigh’s Law after the measure passed the House unanimously. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
He met Kozak about five years ago while running for Arizona attorney general. Years later, as he campaigned for Congress, the two met outside an In-N-Out Burger, where he made her a promise.
"I told Kayleigh, I said, ‘Kayleigh, the moment I get to Congress, it’s going to be one of my first bills that I get done,’" Hamadeh recalled.
Kozak and her children later joined Hamadeh at the Capitol as the House approved the legislation.
"Promise made, promise kept," Hamadeh said. "To actually see it done has been really wonderful."
Hamadeh, a former prosecutor and Army veteran, said Kozak transformed the trauma she endured into a campaign that could protect millions of other survivors.
NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN
Rep. Abe Hamadeh, R-Ariz., poses with Kayleigh Kozak, her husband and their five children following House action on Kayleigh’s Law. (X/@RepAbeHamadeh)
"She’s turned this tragedy into something that’s an inspiration to so many," he said. "From the moment it happened, it’s always been personal to me."
Asked about defendants’ due process rights, Hamadeh noted that the restrictions would apply only after a conviction.
"This is not about the due process beforehand," he said. "They ultimately have to be found guilty of a crime."
Once an offender has been convicted and sentenced, Hamadeh argued, that person should not be allowed to contact the victim or repeatedly summon the survivor back to court.
"The victim shouldn’t be re-traumatized over and over again," he said. "At that point, they should have no ability to contact the victim ever in their lifetime."
AOC OFFERS RARE PRAISE TO LATE SEN GRAHAM FOR BACKING AI PORN BILL NOW STALLED IN HOUSE
Rep. Abe Hamadeh said Kayleigh’s Law would prevent convicted offenders from repeatedly dragging their victims back into court. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Hamadeh said his time as a prosecutor showed him how emotionally punishing the court system can be for survivors forced to revisit deeply personal trauma.
"You have to relive that over and over again," he said.
"Justice is not complete if the victim still lives in fear," Hamadeh said. "Arizona already closed that gap. It is time the federal government did the same."
The legislation now faces the Senate, where Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, is leading the effort to move it forward, according to Hamadeh.
Hamadeh also credited Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., for helping move the measure through the House Judiciary Committee and urged Americans to call on senators to bring it to the floor.
"It passed unanimously in the House. It should pass unanimously in the Senate," Hamadeh said. "We should fix this once and for all and be able to save victims so much of this trauma and this terror."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Hamadeh said he hopes the bill reaches President Donald Trump’s desk before November.
"Call your senators," he said. "Ask them to bring up Kayleigh’s Law to the floor."
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: AOC backs Florida Dem Angie Nixon for US Senate: 'I’m proud to endorse her'
summary: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez endorses Democratic Sunshine State U.S. Senate candidate Florida state Rep. Angie Dixon, who is running against GOP Sen. Ashley Moody.
story: Democratic Florida U.S. Senate candidate Angie Nixon claimed President Donald Trump was pushing communism through his recent deal for Venezuelan oil.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., has endorsed Florida Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Angie Nixon ahead of her November matchup against Republican Sen. Ashley Moody.

"At a time when working families are fighting tooth and nail to make ends meet while the Administration sells them out to corrupt special interests, we need to stand behind leaders who are accountable to working people and stand up to greedy corporations," Ocasio-Cortez said, according to Nixon's campaign.
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment Thursday morning.
PROGRESSIVE FLORIDA DEMOCRAT INSISTS TRUMP WAS PUSHING 'COMMUNISM' WITH VENEZUELA DEAL
U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., speaks to reporters on the House steps after a series of votes at the U.S. Capitol on July 22, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"Angie Nixon will do just that – from fighting for universal healthcare and childcare to proposing a national rent freeze. Angie will be an exemplary fighter for the working families of Florida and will do it all without a dime of corporate PAC money. Angie did not get here by yielding to major political machines, she did it by building community power and by fiercely committing to her values, and that’s why I’m proud to endorse her for the U.S. Senate," Ocasio-Cortez added in the statement issued by Nixon's campaign.
Nixon, a Florida state representative, will face Republican U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody in the special general election contest.

Sunshine State Gov. Ron DeSantis handed Moody a U.S. Senate seat last year. Marco Rubio, who vacated the seat, departed the Senate prior to the end of his term in order to serve as secretary of state.
FLA DEM SEN-NOMINEE ANGIE NIXON BACKED ABOLISHING ELECTORAL COLLEGE, RANKED-CHOICE VOTING IN RESURFACED CLIPS

Democratic U.S. Senate candidate, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon speaks during a visit to the Ball and Chain Cuban restaurant/nightclub as she campaigns in the Little Havana neighborhood on Aug. 29, 2026 in Miami, Fla. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
"I'm honored to have the endorsement of Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and her support as we work towards a better future for Florida," Nixon said, according to her campaign.

"AOC is a fighter and a reminder of what’s possible when you put the needs of the people first, instead of protecting the interests of the wealthy and well-connected. Florida deserves, and is ready for, the kind of leadership in the U.S. Senate that has been absent for far too long. Together, we’re going to fight for everyone: working families, students, and communities who have been ignored for too long. This endorsement adds fuel to an already energized campaign, reinforcing that people are looking forward to real change and representation. I cannot wait to call her my colleague in November," Nixon added.
Moody is backed by President Donald Trump.
AOC CAUGHT OFF GUARD WHEN ASKED BY TMZ WHETHER SHE'D EVER DATE A CONSERVATIVE AFTER REPORTED SPLIT FROM FIANCÉ

title: Her immigrant parents built a NYC grocery store from scratch. Now Mamdani's experiment could end it
summary: Josefina Aguirre's Spanish Harlem meat market faces a taxpayer-backed competitor just two blocks away under Zohran Mamdani's municipal grocery plan.
story: Josefina Aguirre, a first-generation American whose family has run its NYC grocery store for nearly 30 years, says Mamdani’s city-run stores could threaten her livelihood and ultimately force her family out of business.
"It's going to be $1," Josefina Aguirre said to a customer, pausing an interview with Fox News Digital inside her family's Spanish Harlem meat market.

"Okay, I'm sorry. I got a couple of customers. Let's start over," Aguirre, a first-generation American, said. "This is me," she added with a laugh from behind the counter where she has worked for the past 30 years.

Aguirre is among the neighborhood grocers suing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his plan to open city-backed grocery stores across all five boroughs. He says the plan will offer shoppers prices roughly 30% lower than comparable retailers. Local business owners argue it will force small local-run stores to shutter.
EXPERTS SCORCH MAMDANI'S GROCERY PLAN AS AN 'ILLUSION' THAT WILL HAVE TAXPAYERS FOOTING THE BILL
Bodegas and small grocery stores have long been fixtures of New York City neighborhoods, serving generations of residents often just steps from their homes. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
"When we heard Mamdani was opening a grocery store where people are gonna save 30%, it scares us because we don't have the money to compete," Aguirre said.
"I mean, we are New Yorkers, we're not scared of competition, we never have been, but when you have a grocery store coming in like this, it could take us out of business."

One of the proposed city-backed stores is set to open next year at La Marqueta, an existing public market just two blocks from Little Mexico, the family business Aguirre's parents opened in 1997. The city is expected to spend roughly $30 million to build the location, putting a taxpayer-backed competitor practically on Aguirre's doorstep.
NYC TAXPAYERS COULD PAY TWICE UNDER MAMDANI'S CITY-OWNED GROCERY STORE PLAN
A $30 million city-backed grocery store is opening two blocks from NYC grocer Josefina Aguirre’s family business. (Kendall Rodriguez/Newsday RM/Getty Images)
For generations, bodegas and small grocery stores have been woven into the fabric of New York City neighborhoods, serving customers who often live just blocks away.

Aguirre said the shop, which she now runs with her two sisters, has survived the COVID-19 pandemic, rising rents and competition from big-box retailers such as a nearby Costco. But after nearly three decades in business, Aguirre fears Mamdani's city-run grocery plan could be the setback her family cannot survive.
"If I’m selling a whole chicken for $13, and he’s giving it for $7, they’re gonna buy the $7 chicken," Aguirre said. "Who doesn’t want a 30% discount?"
For Aguirre, the stakes extend well beyond losing customers.
"I pay my mortgage from here. I pay for my kid's tuition. This is what I've been doing for over 30 years. Do I need to start over in a new career?"

Aguirre's concerns are at the heart of a lawsuit brought by a group of New York City grocers challenging Mamdani's plan, which would use public money and city resources to create competitors they argue private businesses cannot realistically match.
NYC GROCERS SOUND ALARM ON MAMDANI'S SUPERMARKET PLAN: 'WE'LL LOSE CUSTOMERS'

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has made city-owned grocery stores a centerpiece of his affordability agenda, arguing the government-backed model can deliver lower prices to New Yorkers. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Mamdani has committed $70 million to opening five municipal grocery stores, one in each borough, pitching the model as a way to bring down grocery bills for New Yorkers struggling with the rising cost of food. The stores would operate on city-owned property without having to pay rent or property taxes, advantages Mamdani has argued would allow them to offer lower prices.
Independent grocers argue those same taxpayer-backed advantages would leave businesses like Little Mexico competing on an uneven playing field.

Mamdani's grocery push is also an early test of his broader socialist vision for New York, bringing government-run stores into direct competition with private businesses in a city synonymous with capitalism.
FROM FREE BUSES TO CITY-OWNED GROCERY STORES, HERE ARE MAMDANI’S KEY ECONOMIC PROMISES
For Aguirre, however, the fight is more personal.
"This is what my parents left us," Aguirre said. "It'll be sad to see us leave."
But walking away from the business her family has spent nearly three decades building is the last outcome she wants.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"So what will happen next? The next thing would be closing our business, and we don't want to close, we've been here for years," she said.
Mamdani's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Collins lights up internet with response to Dem challenger fathering children with relative: 'Stone cold'
summary: Susan Collins used a sly rhetorical move to highlight that opponent Troy Jackson fathered two children with his second cousin during a campaign interview.
story: GOP Sen. Susan Collins of Maine told Fox News Digital her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson apparently "struggles to control his temper" in Kittery, Maine, on Aug. 14, 2026.
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, had a sly way of addressing reports that Troy Jackson, her Democratic opponent, fathered two children with his second cousin.

"Well, I'm not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin," Collins told a Politico reporter when asked if Jackson’s personal life would be fair game on the campaign trail. "I don’t know whether people know that or not."
"But you just mentioned it," the reporter shot back.
The clip quickly spread across social media as conservatives praised Collins for her political savvy.
TOP DEM OPERATIVE BRUSHES OFF LATEST SCANDAL PLAGUING MAINE SENATE CANDIDATE AS 'SALACIOUS GOSSIP'

Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, left, is on a glide path to replace former candidate Graham Platner as the Democratic Party's Senate nominee in Maine and face off in the midterm elections against longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images; Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Republican political operative Jesse Hunt reacted to a clip of the interview by calling Collins a "silent killer."
"A less-than-2-minute precis of how Susan Collins is as stone-cold a political combatant as the Senate has ever seen," Politico editor Mike DeBonis wrote on X.

National Rifle Association public affairs director and Maine native Justin Davis responded to the clip by predicting that "the upcoming debates are going to be gold." NOTUS reporter Igor Bobic, meanwhile, said that Collins used a "Trump tactic" by bringing up a subject while pretending not to mention it.
"Count Collins out (like everyone did in ‘20) at your own peril," Targeted Victory CCO Matt Gorman posted on X.
"Susan Collins from the top rope on Troy Jackson," GOP communicator Steve Guest posted on X.
Reports about Jackson’s relationship with his second cousin first surfaced in July, when The Maine Wire reported that Jackson and his longtime partner share the same great-grandparents.
MAINE DEMOCRATS CROWN TROY JACKSON AS PLATNER REPLACEMENT AS FRESH SCRUTINY CLOUDS SENATE RESET
Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, departs the chamber at the Capitol in Washington, on July 24, 2025. (J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo)

"It's truly hysterical how Democrats can't seem to find one normal dude to run for office," conservative commentator Greg Price posted on X, alluding to the fact that Jackson replaced Graham Platner on the ballot in Maine after he terminated his campaign amid a rape allegation.

Other aspects of Jackson’s personal life have come to the forefront of his Senate campaign, including a 1988 police report which claims he assaulted a man at a bar. The report also states that his partner accused him of pushing her around.
Jackson does not dispute that he attacked another man, but strongly denies laying a hand on his partner, who has said she does not recall giving a statement to that effect to the police.

When asked about the police report in August, Collins told Fox News Digital that "he’s the one that needs to respond to the reports. I’m not going to comment on them. But I will say that based on widespread reporting it appears that he struggles to control his temper ... From my perspective, it seems that vetting is very important. We learned the failure of vetting with Graham Platner. But that’s really up to the Democrats."
EMBATTLED MAINE DEMOCRAT DEADLOCKED WITH COLLINS DESPITE CONTROVERSIES IN KEY SENATE RACE, NEW POLL SHOWS

Troy Jackson speaks as he became the Maine Democratic Party's choice to be their U.S. Senate nominee to replace Graham Platner on the ballot in November on July 25, 2026, in Bangor, Maine. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

During her interview with Politico, Collins denied that Jackson would necessarily be an easier opponent than Platner, pointing out that the former has a long political record that he can be criticized over — something that Platner lacked as a political outsider.
Jackson has framed the GOP focus on his personal life as a distraction from the issues Mainers actually care about.

"Susan Collins will do anything to distract from the fact that she votes with Trump 96% of the time and has sold out working people in Maine," his campaign previously told Fox News Digital. "Personal attacks on Troy's family are shameful and desperate."

The Jackson campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Wednesday.
Fox News Digital's Paul Steinhauser contributed to this report.

title: MAGA begins to crack as 2026 GOP roster backs away from Trump's tech vision
summary: Donald Trump urges communities to "let Data Reign," but GOP candidates across battleground states propose data center moratoriums ahead of midterms.
story: A growing number of Republicans running in this year’s midterm elections are taping the brakes on new AI data center construction following voter backlash.

With a slew of polls showing that most Americans oppose the construction in their communities of new data centers to power AI, a growing number of Republicans running in this year's elections are putting daylight between themselves and President Donald Trump.

Trump, a strong proponent of data center development, took to social media Monday to argue that if communities "want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign."

But with GOP strategists warning that data centers have become politically radioactive, some Republicans on the midterm ballot are reversing course, which is a stark shift for a party that previously had fully embraced the burgeoning AI industry.

Seventy percent of voters questioned in a recent Fox News poll said they wanted to hit the brakes on building data centers in their area to support artificial intelligence, with only 30% in favor. Only 40% of Republicans, and 46% of MAGA Republicans supported new data center construction.
CRUCIAL SENATE RACE ERUPTS OVER AI'S MASSIVE ENERGY APPETITE
Fueling the opposition are concerns over rising electricity costs and energy and water consumption.

"I think we need to take a pause, probably, and make sure that we're answering all the questions that people have on them," former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP Senate nominee in battleground Michigan, said two weeks ago when asked about data center construction.

Rogers, who previously welcomed data center expansion in Michigan, later outlined a one-year moratorium, arguing that "Michigan needs stronger guardrails to protect community control, prevent utility price hikes, protect our water, and stop pay-to-play schemes."
DEMOCRAT FETTERMAN ALIGNS WITH TRUMP ON AI ARGUMENT

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, announces support for a one-year moratorium on new data center construction, on August 20, 2026, in Detroit, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
He's far from alone.

In Ohio's crucial Senate race between appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted and his Democratic challenger, former longtime Sen. Sherrod Brown, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) warned that the issue could help the Democrats flip the seat. Brown and allied groups have shelled out millions of dollars to run ads calling Husted "the face of data centers in Ohio."
"More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck," the NRSC memo emphasized.
Husted has introduced a Senate bill to stop average Americans from paying for data center energy costs.
BERNIE SANDERS: 'WE MUST HIT THE PAUSE ON AI BEFORE IT'S TOO LATE'

Volunteers hand out yard signs against a data center complex in Canaan Valley on June 30, 2025, after a public meeting organized by the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection regarding an air quality permit application for a gas-fired power plant near Davis, W. Va. (ULYSSE BELLIER/AFP via Getty Images)
The political pushback stretches well beyond Michigan and Ohio.
Texas Attorney General and U.S. Senate nominee Ken Paxton last month unveiled a four-point plan to curb rapid data center growth and address public concerns over resource strain.
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican running for a fourth term steering the Lone Star State, halted new data center connections to the state's power grid pending a comprehensive regulatory audit.

Ohio Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy pledged to issue a first-day-in-office executive order halting approval of all new data center projects until his proposed safeguards are enacted.

Rep. Tom Tiffany, the GOP nominee for governor in swing state Wisconsin, has highlighted that he opposes new data centers unless strict conditions are met. Tiffany has made data centers a centerpiece of his gubernatorial campaign, slamming his Democratic rival, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, as "Data Center David Crowley."
Pennsylvania Treasurer and Republican gubernatorial nominee Stacy Garrity has called for a temporary pause on new and uncontracted major data center developments in her battleground state.

Other Republicans are stopping short of moratoriums. Rep. Byron Donalds, the GOP gubernatorial nominee who opposes bans or moratoriums and whose primary campaign received significant backing from the AI industry, introduced legislation this summer that would require large AI data centers to generate their own power and water rather than draw from public utilities.
COOL YOUR SERVERS: CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POLL ON AI DATA CENTERS
Trump is standing firm.
The president recently called Abbott's decision to pump the brakes on data center development a "mistake."
And Trump, on Monday said, "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame."
The president, who has made data centers a key ingredient in winning the AI race with China, argued: "China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement."
But Trump, at least for now, seems to be giving Republicans some wiggle room.
"If a Republican’s against a data center, that’s OK with me," Trump said.
Veteran Republican strategist Matt Gorman told Fox News Digital that "Trump is smartly taking the long view of this."
Gorman said "Republicans on the ballot this year are being responsive to the very real concerns people have," adding that "these companies and their champions have to do more to make the case."
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
An Amazon Web Services data center in Aldie, Virginia, on May 31, 2026. (Lexi Critchett/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The AI industry is responding to the political backlash.

Build American AI, an industry-aligned group powered by top AI leaders, this week launched a multimillion-dollar public engagement campaign to build support for "clear, strong, and commonsense policies governing the development of the data centers and energy infrastructure."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

It highlighted that the "policies should protect residential ratepayers, safeguard the environment and water resources, require developers to pay their fair share, and preserve the right of every community to decide whether it wants to welcome data center investment."

"We can protect ratepayers, safeguard our natural resources, respect the right of communities to decide whether they want to welcome this investment, and still build the infrastructure America needs to lead the world in artificial intelligence," Build American AI added.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Johnson downplays GOP's midterm woes as Democrats eye House takeover: 'I am very bullish'
summary: With Election Day two months away, Democrats eye Senate and House majorities as inflation, gas prices and Trump's approval ratings batter the GOP.
story: Asked about not only holding but growing the GOP’s congressional majority, House Speaker Mike Johnson tells News Digital ‘I am very bullish about the outcome on Election Night.’
With two months to go until Election Day, and early voting kicking off later this month in half a dozen states, Democrats are increasingly optimistic they can recapture congressional majorities.

With the final stretch towards the midterms underway, Democrats see an unexpectedly favorable political environment despite their own weak national brand, while Republicans insist structural advantages and the Democrats' shift to the left will allow them to defy midterm history.

Senate Republicans control their chamber by a 53-47 margin, and the majority is even more fragile in the House. And the latest forecasts from the leading nonpartisan political handicappers keep leaning towards the Democrats.
But a defiant House Speaker Mike Johnson not only predicts the GOP will hold control of the chamber, but he tells Fox News Digital, "We're going to grow the majority."
SPEAKER JOHNSON'S MIDTERM PREDICTION TO BUCK HISTORY

House Speaker Mike Johnson, center, campaigns with former Gov. Paul LePage, the Republican nominee in Maine's 2nd Congressional District, in Auburn, Maine, on August 17, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Republicans — as the party currently in power — were already up against traditional political headwinds that have historically led to a loss of congressional seats during midterm election years. Add to that the challenging climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see daily at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and President Donald Trump's well underwater approval ratings.

"We are going to take back the Senate. Republicans thought they had the Senate locked down, but now Democrats, we are on the path to victory. We've blown the map wide open," longtime Senate Democratic Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York told reporters two weeks ago.

But Democrats have problems of their own as they try to win back control of congressional majorities in the midterms, including a party brand that public opinion polling indicates is extremely unpopular. And high-profile victories this spring and summer by left-wing and socialist candidates over establishment rivals in Democratic primaries are giving Republicans extra ammunition to portray all Democrats as extremists.
THESE 12 MIDTERM RACES WILL DECIDE WHICH PARTY CONTROLS THE SENATE

Congressional candidate Claire Valdez, congressional candidate Brad Lander, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier raise their hands during a Get Out the Vote (GOTV) rally at King's Theater on June 18, 2026, in New York City. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

"It's a contrast election, and people are making a contrast between common-sense solutions and candidates, and really crazy, which is represented by the other side," Johnson claimed, during a Fox News Digital interview on the campaign trail in Maine. "I am very bullish about the outcome on election night."

In the battle for the House, the mid-decade redistricting push by Trump and GOP leaders is giving Republicans a boost, with a potential net gain of up to a dozen newly drawn right-tilting districts across the country.

But in a sign of the rough landscape facing the GOP, House Democrats last month expanded their midterm target list to 58 Republican-held districts, including 12 seats in territory Trump carried in 2024.
The victories by Trump and Republicans two years ago were fueled by Americans fed up with the high cost of living. Two years later, inflation is the Republicans' biggest liability.
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

President Donald Trump points as he arrives to speak during a campaign rally for U.S. Sen. Darline Graham at Myrtle Beach Convention Center in Myrtle Beach, S.C. on Aug. 21, 2026. (SAUL LOEB / AFP via Getty Images)
Three out of four voters questioned in the most recent Fox News national poll said inflation had caused financial hardship, while 54% expected the economy to worsen.

The Fox News poll and other recent surveys also indicate Democrats holding an enthusiasm advantage over Republicans, and continuing to lead on the generic ballot question, which asks if a respondent would vote for the Democrat or Republican in their congressional district without offering specific names.

"Donald Trump started a war that no one wanted, and now Americans are paying the price. Gas prices are soaring and families who were already struggling in Trump’s economy are forced to stretch their budgets even further while footing the bill for this war," Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said in a statement.
Republicans hold a campaign cash edge over Democrats, and remain optimistic about the midterms.
"We have a chance to defy history and win the midterms," Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters told Fox News Digital this summer.
Gruters and other GOP leaders are spotlighting the major tax cuts on tips, overtime and Social Security that congressional Republicans passed and Trump signed into law last year.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
But Republicans are facing a low-propensity problem: MAGA voters who don't always go to the polls when Trump's name isn't on the ballot.

Gruters called Trump the "best showman that's ever existed in politics, bar none... He knows how to deliver these low-propensity voters. He knows how to get people up, motivated, excited about the midterms, and that's what we're going to need."

And he pointed to next week's first ever GOP midterm convention and said, "It gives us a chance to highlight all the wonderful things this president has done in our effort on this great American comeback."

Trump, at a White House dinner with Republican leaders on Wednesday evening, pledged that he'll be on the midterm campaign trail: "I'm going to take the final 30 days, maybe a little bit more than that, because it's all about 35 races."

Democrats are touting their own get-out-the-vote efforts.

"This year, the DNC organizing team launched Local Listeners, a first-of-its-kind program that talked to nearly 10,000 people who voted in 2020, but not 2024," the DNC's Martin said. "What we found could change the game for the midterms this year."
